title: High and Behind the Wheel: Why Not | The Bridge
h1: High and Behind the Wheel: Why Not
description: Cannabis is legal in New York. Driving on it isn't. What the law says, what it costs, what it does to your driving, and how to plan ahead.
lede: Cannabis is legal in New York. Driving on it isn't, and there's no gray area to argue about at the side of the road.
html:
"If you feel different, you drive different." That's New York's own line, and it's about as good as public safety copy gets. Cannabis is legal here for adults. Driving on it is not, medical patient or otherwise, and nothing about the 2021 law changed that.

What it costs

Impaired driving under the influence of cannabis is a misdemeanor under Vehicle and Traffic Law section 1192. The DMV's penalty table for driving while impaired by a drug reads like this:

  • First violation: $500 to $1,000 fine, up to a year in jail, license revoked for at least six months.
  • Second within 10 years: a felony, $1,000 to $5,000, up to four years, license revoked for at least a year.
  • Third within 10 years: a higher felony, $2,000 to $10,000, up to seven years, license revoked for at least a year.

Add alcohol to the mix and there's a combination charge with the same ranges. Three or more alcohol or drug-related convictions or refusals in 10 years can mean permanent revocation.

What's legal in the car

You can carry legal amounts: up to 3 ounces of cannabis and 24 grams of concentrated cannabis. It has to stay closed. No open containers or packaging, for the driver or the passengers. No smoking in the vehicle by anyone, moving or parked, so sitting at the curb doesn't get you around it. So if you've just left a dispensary, the package stays sealed until you're home.

The 2021 law limits how police can use the smell of cannabis to justify a search. That protection has an exception for investigating a driver under the influence, so don't count on it behind the wheel.

What it does to your driving

The CDC says cannabis affects the parts of the brain that control movement, balance, coordination, memory and judgment. It can slow your reaction time and decision making, impair coordination and distort perception. The National Institute on Drug Abuse reports more lane weaving, poorer reaction time and altered attention to the road, and more weaving still when alcohol is added.

Straight facts: the crash numbers are messier than either side likes. NIDA cites several studies finding that drivers with THC in their blood were roughly twice as likely to be responsible for a deadly crash or to be killed, and a large federal study that found no significant increase in risk after controlling for things like age and alcohol. It says more research is needed. That isn't a permission slip. A slower foot on the brake doesn't wait for the literature, and the law applies either way.

Why there's no math for this

People want a rule of thumb, some number of hours or a number of hits. There isn't one. The CDC says it's difficult to connect the concentration of THC to impairment for an individual person, and NIDA notes THC can be detected in body fluids for days or even weeks after use. The state's guidance doesn't give you a number of hours. It says if you're not sure, stay put.

Timing makes it worse. The state's guide says inhaled cannabis comes on in about seven to ten minutes and lasts one to three hours, while edibles last four to twelve. And an edible, the state warns, can take as long as four hours to take effect. You can feel fine pulling out of the driveway and not feel fine on the highway.

The plan

Settle the ride home first, not after. Take the train or the bus. Get a ride from someone sober. Or stay where you are. Don't get in with a driver who's high, and don't let a friend drive that way if you can stop it. The state's guide files this under consuming responsibly, right next to knowing your serving size.

One more thing, said without judgment. The state lists using cannabis in high-risk situations, like driving, among the signs of cannabis use disorder. If that's become routine, New York's HOPE Line runs 24 hours a day: call 1-877-846-7369 or text HOPENY (467369). More on how it all works is on our Facts page.
